content_voiceover: This page presents two more high yield questions. Question twenty asks which statement about targeted therapies in AML is wrong, and the answer is the statement about quizartinib. Quizartinib is actually a first generation, type two FLT3 inhibitor, and its pivotal trial combining it with standard seven plus three induction enrolled only patients with FLT3 internal tandem duplication, not FLT3 TKD mutations, so claiming a survival benefit across both mutation types is incorrect. The other statements about glasdegib, gilteritinib, midostaurin, and gilteritinib maintenance based on measurable residual disease status are all accurate. Question twenty seven asks which statement about acute promyelocytic leukemia is wrong, and the answer concerns variant RARA translocations. While the classic translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 produces the PML RARA fusion that responds beautifully to ATRA, variant translocation partners such as NPM1, NUMA1, ZBTB16, and STAT5B do not all respond well to ATRA, in fact the ZBTB16 and STAT5B fusions are well known to confer ATRA resistance, so it is wrong to say all variant translocations respond effectively to ATRA therapy.
keypoints: Quizartinib is a first-generation, type II FLT3 inhibitor tested only in FLT3-ITD disease
APL classically shows t(15;17) producing the PML-RARA fusion, highly ATRA-sensitive
Variant RARA fusion partners like ZBTB16 and STAT5B confer ATRA resistance
Not all APL variant translocations respond equally well to ATRA
keypoint_voiceover: Two traps to remember, quizartinib's proven benefit is specific to FLT3 ITD disease, not TKD. And in APL, while classic PML RARA responds beautifully to ATRA, variant partners like ZBTB16 and STAT5B are known to be ATRA resistant.
